problem.text: A moving particle starts at the point $(4, 4)$ and moves until it hits one of the coordinate axes for the first time. When the particle is at the point $(a, b)$, it moves at random to one of the points $(a-1, b)$, $(a, b-1)$, or $(a-1, b-1)$, each with probability $\frac{1}{3}$, independently of its previous moves. The probability that it will hit the coordinate axes at $(0, 0)$ is $\frac{m}{3^n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are positive integers such that $m$ is not divisible by $3$. Find $m + n$.

steps.title: Where to start: look at the very last move
steps.body: The particle stops the first time it touches an axis, so to end at $(0, 0)$ it must not touch an axis anywhere earlier. Ask which points can move into $(0, 0)$: only $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 1)$.

your_turn.prompt: Why can the particle not arrive at $(0, 0)$ from $(1, 0)$ or $(0, 1)$?
your_turn.answer: Those points are on the axes, so the particle would already have stopped there. The last move must be the diagonal move from $(1, 1)$.

steps.title: Turn the trip to $(1, 1)$ into words
steps.body: Call the moves L for $(a-1, b)$, D for $(a, b-1)$ and C for the diagonal $(a-1, b-1)$. Going from $(4, 4)$ to $(1, 1)$ lowers each coordinate by $3$, and both coordinates only go down, so the particle stays at least $1$ away from both axes on the way. If the trip uses $k$ C moves, it needs $3 - k$ L moves and $3 - k$ D moves, for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$. Each move has probability $\frac{1}{3}$, so one particular sequence of $6 - k$ moves has probability $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{6-k}$.

your_turn.prompt: For $k = 1$, how many moves does the trip take, and what is the probability of one particular sequence such as LLDDC?

steps.title: Count the words in each case
steps.body: The number of orders is the number of ways to rearrange the letters. For $k = 0$ the word LLLDDD has $\frac{6!}{3!\,3!} = 20$ arrangements, and for $k = 3$ the word CCC has just $1$. So these two cases give probabilities $\frac{20}{3^6}$ and $\frac{1}{3^3}$.

your_turn.prompt: Count the arrangements of LLDDC ($k = 1$) and of LDCC ($k = 2$).

steps.title: Use one common denominator
steps.body: The four cases cannot happen together, so their probabilities add. To add them, write every fraction over $3^6$.

your_turn.answer: $\frac{90}{3^6}$, $\frac{108}{3^6}$ and $\frac{27}{3^6}$ (multiply top and bottom by $3$, $9$ and $27$).

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: The chance of reaching $(1, 1)$ is $\frac{20 + 90 + 108 + 27}{3^6} = \frac{245}{3^6}$. The final C move from $(1, 1)$ has probability $\frac{1}{3}$, so the answer to the probability question is $\frac{245}{3^7}$. Since $245 = 5\cdot 7^2$ is not divisible by $3$, we have $m = 245$ and $n = 7$, so $m + n = 252$. The answer is **$252$**.
